Derbyshire|Desmond Derbyshire]] [[Christopher Potts]] | known_for = {{Plainlist| * ''[[The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language]]'' * [[Language Log]]}} | awards = {{Plainlist| * [[Leonard Bloomfield Book Award]] (2004; shared with [[Rodney Huddleston]]) * [[Linguistics, Language, and the Public Award]] (2009; shared with [[Mark Liberman]])}} | website = {{Official URL}} | spouse = {{Plainlist| * Joan E. Rainford (1967–93) * [[Barbara Scholz|Barbara C. Scholz]] (1994–2011) * Patricia C. Shannon (2014–2016)}} | partner = [[Joan Maling]] }} {{Infobox musical artist | name = Geoffrey Keith Pullum | alias = Jeff Wright | instrument = Keyboard | years_active = 1961–1967 | label = [[Piccadilly Records|Piccadilly]] | past_member_of = {{Plainlist| * Sonny Stewart and the Dynamos * [[Geno Washington & the Ram Jam Band]]}} }} '''Geoffrey Keith Pullum''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|p|ʊ|l|əm}}; born 8 March 1945) is a British and American [[linguist]] specialising in the study of [[English language|English]]. Pullum has published over 300 articles and books on various topics in linguistics, including phonology, morphology, semantics, pragmatics, computational linguistics, and philosophy of language. He is Professor Emeritus of General Linguistics at the [[University of Edinburgh]].{{Cite web|title=Geoffrey K Pullum|url=https://www.ed.ac.uk/profile/geoffrey-k-pullum|access-date=2021-05-27|website=The University of Edinburgh|date=11 June 2020 |language=en}} Pullum is a co-author of ''[[The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language]]'' (2002),{{cite book|last1=Huddleston|first1=Rodney|title=The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language|last2=Pullum|first2=Geoffrey K.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2002|isbn=978-0-521-43146-0|location=Cambridge; New York|page=|author-link=Rodney Huddleston|author-link2=Geoffrey Pullum}} a comprehensive [[Linguistic description|descriptive grammar]] of English. He was co-founder of ''[[Language Log]]'' and a contributor to Lingua Franca at ''[[The Chronicle of Higher Education]]'', often criticizing prescriptive rules and linguistic myths. == Early life == Geoffrey K. Pullum was born in [[Irvine, North Ayrshire]], Scotland, on 8 March 1945, and moved to [[West Wickham]], England, while very young. == Career as a musician == He left secondary school at age 16 and toured Germany as a pianist in the rock and roll band [[Sonny Stewart and the Dynamos]]. A year and a half later, he returned to England and co-founded a soul band with [[Pete Gage (guitarist)|Pete Gage]], which became [[Geno Washington & the Ram Jam Band]] when [[Geno Washington]] joined.{{cite book |title=[[Encyclopedia of Popular Music|The Virgin Encyclopedia of Popular Music]] |date=1997 |publisher=[[Virgin Books]] |isbn=1-85227-745-9 |editor=Colin Larkin |editor-link=Colin Larkin (writer) |edition=Concise |page=1234}} Pullum went by the name of Jeff Wright.{{Cite web |title=Geno Washington & The Ram Jam Band 1965-1967 |url=https://thestrangebrew.co.uk/interviews/geno-washington-the-ram-jam-band/ |access-date=2023-07-01 |website=The Strange Brew |language=en-GB}} The group had two of the biggest selling UK albums of the 1960s, both of which were live albums. Their most commercially successful album, ''Hand Clappin, Foot Stompin, Funky-Butt ... Live!'', was in the [[UK Albums Chart]] for 38 weeks in 1966 and 1967, peaking at number 5. The other album was ''Hipster Flipsters Finger Poppin' Daddies'', which reached number 8 on the same chart.Martin Roach (ed.), ''Virgin Book of British Hit Albums'', 2009, p.292 The singles included "[[Water (Miller & Atkins song)|Water]]", "[[Hi Hi Hazel]]", "[[Que Sera, Sera (Whatever Will Be, Will Be)|Que Sera Sera]]" and "[[Michael (the Lover)]]".{{Cite web |title=Geno Washington and His Ram Jam Band {{!}} full Official Chart History |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/12522/geno-washington-and-his-ram-jam-band/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=Official Charts}} == Education == After the band broke up, Pullum enrolled in the [[University of York]] in 1968, graduating in 1972 with a Bachelor of Arts with first class honours. In 1976 he completed a PhD in [[Linguistics]] at [[University College London]], where his thesis supervisor was [[Neil Smith (linguist)|Neil Smith]].{{Cite book |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |url=http://archive.org/details/ruleinteractiono0000pull |title=Rule interaction and the organization of a grammar |date=1979 |location=New York | publisher=Garland |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-8240-9668-7}} == Career as a linguist == Pullum's work in the 1970s with [[Desmond C. Derbyshire|Desmond Derbyshire]], for whom he was the primary doctoral supervisor, established the existence of [[Object–verb–subject word order|object-initial languages]].{{Cite journal |last1=Derbyshire |first1=Desmond C. |last2=Pullum |first2=Geoffrey |date=1979-01-01 |title=Object initial languages |journal=Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session |volume=23 |issue=1 |doi=10.31356/silwp.vol23.02 |issn=0361-4700|doi-access=free }} Pullum left Britain in 1980, taking visiting positions at the [[University of Washington]] and [[Stanford University]]. He contributed significantly to the development of [[Generalized phrase structure grammar|Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar]].{{Cite book |first1=Gerald |last1=Gazdar |title=Generalized phrase structure grammar |last2=Klein |first2=Ewan |last3=Pullum |first3=Geoffrey K. |last4=Sag |first4=Ivan A. |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts | publisher=Harvard University Press |year=1985 |isbn=0-674-34455-3 |oclc=644797704}} In 1983, he and [[Arnold Zwicky]] showed that ''[[English auxiliary verbs|n't]]'' is a negative inflectional morpheme, and not simply a [[Contraction (grammar)|contraction]] of ''not''.{{Cite journal |last1=Zwicky |first1=Arnold M. |last2=Pullum |first2=Geoffrey K. |year=1983 |title=Cliticization vs. inflection: English N'T |url= |journal=Language |volume=59 |issue=3 |pages=502–513 |doi=10.2307/413900 |jstor=413900 |issn=}} In 1987, he became a [[Citizenship in the United States|United States citizen]]. He worked at the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]], from 1981 to 2007.{{Cite web|title=Geoffrey K. Pullum: Redirect|url=https://people.ucsc.edu/~pullum/|access-date=2021-05-27|website=UCSC}} He was Dean of Graduate Studies and Research from 1987 to 1993.{{Cite web |title=Academy of Europe: Pullum Geoffrey |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Pullum_Geoffrey |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=Academia Europaea}} From 1983 to 1989, he wrote the regular "Topic Comment" pieces in ''Natural Language and Linguistic Theory.'' In 1995, Pullum started to collaborate with [[Rodney Huddleston]] and other linguists on ''[[The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language]]'',{{Cite journal|last=Culicover|first=Peter W.|date=2004|title=The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language (review)|url=http://muse.jhu.edu/content/crossref/journals/language/v080/80.1culicover.pdf|journal=Language|language=en|volume=80|issue=1|pages=127–141|doi=10.1353/lan.2004.0018|s2cid=140478848 |issn=1535-0665}} which was published in 2002 and won the [[Leonard Bloomfield Book Award]] of the [[Linguistic Society of America]] in 2004.{{Cite web|title=Leonard Bloomfield Book Award Previous Holders|url=http://www.linguisticsociety.org/content/leonard-bloomfield-book-award-previous-holders|access-date=August 18, 2015|website=Linguistic Society of America}} From 1998 until 2002, he produced 10 "Lingua Franca" talks for the [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]].{{Cite web |title=ABC Search |url=https://discover.abc.net.au/index.html#/?query=Lingua%20Franca%20geoff%20pullum&page=1 |access-date=2023-04-03 |website=ABC}} In 2000, he published, in the style of [[Dr. Seuss]], a proof of [[Turing]]'s theorem that the [[halting problem]] is recursively unsolvable.Pullum, Geoffrey K. (2000) "Scooping the loop snooper: An elementary proof of the undecidability of the halting problem". ''Mathematics Magazine'' 73.4 (October 2000), 319–320. A corrected version appears on the author's website as [http://www.lel.ed.ac.uk/~gpullum/loopsnoop.html "Scooping the loop snooper: A proof that the Halting Problem is undecidable"]. In 2003, he was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].{{Cite web|title=Geoffrey Keith Pullum|url=https://www.amacad.org/person/geoffrey-keith-pullum|access-date=2021-05-27|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|language=en}} In 2004, [[Barbara Scholz]], Pullum, and James Rogers initiated a group project on the applications of [[model theory]] in syntax, which was supported by the [[Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study]] at [[Harvard University]] in 2005–2006.{{Cite web |date=2012-03-16 |title=Barbara C. Scholz |url=https://www.radcliffe.harvard.edu/people/barbara-c-scholz |access-date=2020-03-23 |website=Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University |language=en}} In 2007, he moved to the School of Philosophy, Psychology and Language Sciences, [[University of Edinburgh]], where he was Professor of General Linguistics and at one time Head of Linguistics and English Language. In 2009 he was elected a Fellow of the [[British Academy]],{{Cite web |title=Professor Geoffrey K Pullum FBA |url=https://www.thebritishacademy.ac.uk/fellows/geoffrey-k-pullum-FBA/ |access-date=2021-05-27 |website=The British Academy |language=en}} and, in 2019, a Member of [[Academia Europaea]]. He became emeritus professor in 2020.{{Cite web |title=Geoffrey K Pullum |url=https://www.ed.ac.uk/profile/geoffrey-k-pullum |access-date=2023-04-03 |website=The University of Edinburgh |date=11 June 2020 |language=en}} === Views === ==== Linguistic theory ==== Pullum argues against the view that the "languages"—in the sense of entities like Romanian or English—are scientifically and concretely definable objects. It's this notion of language that is commonly referred to in generative linguistics as ''E-language''.{{Cite book |last1=Daniela |first1=Isac |title=I-language: An Introduction to Linguistics as Cognitive Science |last2=Reiss |first2=Charles |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2008 |isbn=978-0-19-966017-9 |location=Oxford |pages=13 |oclc=829793847}}
It seems to me that the notion of 'a language' should not be regarded as scientifically reconstructable at all. We can say in very broad terms that a human language is a characteristic way of structuring expressions shared by a speech community; but that is extremely vague, and has to remain so. The vagueness is ineliminable, and unproblematic. Human languages are no more scientifically definable than human cultures, ethnic groups, or cities. The most we can say about what it means to say of a person that they speak Japanese is that the person knows, at least to some approximation, how to structure linguistic expressions in the Japanese way (with object before verb, and postpositions, and so on). But in scientific terms there is no such object as 'Japanese'.{{Cite journal |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |title=The central question in comparative syntactic metatheory |url= |journal=Mind & Language |year=2013 |publication-date=2013 |volume=28 |issue=4 |pages=492–521 |doi=10.1111/mila.12029 |issn=}}
Nevertheless, it does not follow for Pullum that an externalist notion of 'language' cannot in principle be an object of scientific study{{Citation |last=Scholz |first=Barbara C. |title=Philosophy of Linguistics |date=2025 |work=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first=Edward N. |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2025/entries/linguistics/ |access-date=2025-06-25 |edition=Summer 2025 |publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University |last2=Pelletier |first2=Francis Jeffry |last3=Pullum |first3=Geoffrey K. |last4=Nefdt |first4=Ryan |editor2-last=Nodelman |editor2-first=Uri}} (cf. Chomsky's perspective that the only scientifically interesting conception of language is an internalist one{{Cite book |last=Chomsky |first=Noam |title=Language and problems of knowledge: the Managua lectures |date=2003 |publisher=MIT Pr |isbn=978-0-262-53070-5 |edition=13. [pr.] |series=Current studies in linguistics series |location=Cambridge, Mass.}}). Instead, Pullum justifies a conception of the grammar that makes claims directly about linguistic expressions, as opposed to sets of such expressions. Pullum advocates for a ''[[Model-theoretic grammar|model-theoretic]]'' conception of grammar under which sentences or expressions are taken to be well-formed if and only if they satisfy necessary conditions on the syntactic structures of individual expressions.{{Cite journal |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |last2=Scholz |first2=Barbara C. |date=2001 |editor-last=de Groote |editor-first=Philippe |editor2-last=Morrill |editor2-first=Glyn |editor3-last=Retoré |editor3-first=Christian |title=On the Distinction between Model-Theoretic and Generative-Enumerative Syntactic Frameworks |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-48199-0_2 |journal=Logical Aspects of Computational Linguistics |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=17–43 |doi=10.1007/3-540-48199-0_2 |isbn=978-3-540-48199-7}} This approach stands in contrast to a ''generative-enumerative'' (or ''proof-theoretic''{{Cite book |last=Tomalin |first=Marcus |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/linguistics-and-the-formal-sciences/9ADCCE0D4CF143A9367718EC73DE5CB4 |title=Linguistics and the Formal Sciences: The Origins of Generative Grammar |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-85481-8 |series=Cambridge Studies in Linguistics |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/cbo9780511486340}}) conception under which a grammar is a recursive procedure that defines a set of well-formed expressions—that is, the full set of expressions that are well-formed in the 'language', and no-more. The upshot of this is that model-theoretic grammars, unlike generative-enumerative grammars, remain silent on the cardinality of the set of well-formed sentences according to the grammar. Pullum takes the answers to such questions in the context of natural language to be unknowable. Hence, a grammar that makes no ontological commitment regarding the (in)finitude of natural language is preferable to one that does.{{Cite journal |last=Nefdt |first=Ryan Mark |date=2024-12-20 |title=Pullum’s philosophy of linguistics: towards a unified framework |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0022226724000240/type/journal_article |journal=Journal of Linguistics |language=en |pages=1–14 |doi=10.1017/S0022226724000240 |issn=0022-2267}}
Grammars of this sort [MTS] are entirely independent of the numerosity of expressions... The constraints are satisfied by expressions with the relevant structure whether there are infinitely many of them, or a huge finite number, or only a few.”{{Citation |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |title=6. Recursion and the infinitude claim |date=2010-03-26 |work=Recursion and Human Language |pages=111–138 |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110219258.111/html |access-date=2025-06-25 |publisher=De Gruyter Mouton |language=en |doi=10.1515/9783110219258.111 |isbn=978-3-11-021925-8 |last2=Scholz |first2=Barbara C.}}
Pullum's grammatical frameworks, such as that in ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language'', have been monotonic [[Phrase structure grammar|phrase-structure grammars]], similar to [[X-bar theory]] but with explicit notation for [[Grammatical relation|syntactic functions]] such as subject, modifier, and complement.{{Cite book |last1=Pullum |first1=Geoffrey K. |url=http://www.lel.ed.ac.uk/~gpullum/EssexLAGB.pdf |title=Annual Meeting of the Linguistics Association of Great Britain |last2=Rogers |first2=James |year=2009 |pages=1–16 |chapter=Expressive power of the syntactic theory implicit in ''The Cambridge Grammar of the English Language''}} Monotonic phrase-structure grammars are based on the idea that the structure of sentences can be represented as a hierarchy of constituents, with each level of the hierarchy corresponding to a different level of grammatical organization. X-bar theory is a specific type of phrase-structure grammar that posits a uniform structure for all phrasal categories, with each phrase containing a "head" and optional specifier and/or complement. The key difference between monotonic phrase-structure grammars and generative grammars like transformational-generative grammar (TGG) is the absence of transformations or movement operations in the former. Monotonic grammars maintain that the structure of a sentence remains fixed from its initial formation, whereas generative grammars propose that sentences can undergo various transformations during the derivation process. Pullum argues that the traditional notion of a [[noun phrase]] is correct, and that the so-called [[Determiner phrase|DP hypothesis]] is mistaken.{{Cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Philip |last2=Pullum |first2=Geoffrey K. |date=2022-10-14 |title=La tête du groupe nominal: l'hypothèse du DP dans les théories génératives |journal=Corela |issue=HS-37 |doi=10.4000/corela.15038 |s2cid=253050932 |issn=1638-573X|doi-access=free }} He believes that some kind of fusion of functions accounts for some of the data leading to the disagreement.{{Cite journal |last1=Payne |first1=John |last2=Huddleston |first2=Rodney |last3=Pullum |first3=Geoffrey K. |title=Fusion of functions: The syntax of ''once'', ''twice'' and ''thrice'' |journal=Journal of Linguistics |year=2007 |publication-date=2007 |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=565–603 |doi=10.1017/s002222670700477x |s2cid=145799573 |issn=0022-2267}} ==== Criticism of Chomsky ==== Pullum has been a long-time critic of [[Noam Chomsky]], whom he accuses of mendacity, plagiarism, and general academic dishonesty.{{Cite magazine |date=2022-02-17 |title=Chomsky's forever war |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/magazine/2022/03/07/chomskys-forever-war/ |access-date=2023-04-02 |magazine=National Review |language=en-US}} He has attacked the argument from the [[poverty of the stimulus]] in multiple publications.{{Cite journal |last=Pullum |first=Geoffrey K. |date=1996-09-25 |title=Learnability, hyperlearning, and the poverty of the stimulus |journal=Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages=498 |doi=10.3765/bls.v22i1.1336 |issn=2377-1666|doi-access=free }}{{Cite journal |last1=Pullum |first1=Geoffrey K |last2=Scholz |first2=Barbara C |date=2002-01-26 |title=Empirical assessment of stimulus poverty arguments |journal=The Linguistic Review |volume=18 |issue=1–2 |doi=10.1515/tlir.19.1-2.9 |s2cid=143735248 |issn=0167-6318}}{{Cite journal |last1=Scholz |first1=Barbara C |last2=Pullum |first2=Geoffrey K |date=2002-01-26 |title=Searching for arguments to support linguistic nativism |journal=The Linguistic Review |volume=18 |issue=1–2 |doi=10.1515/tlir.19.1-2.185 |s2cid=14589503 |issn=0167-6318|citeseerx=10.1.1.562.7362 }} He has called Chomsky's [[Minimalist program|Minimalist Program]] "really just a repertoire of hints, suggestions, and buzzwords", has said that concepts such as [[Deep structure and surface structure|Deep Structure]] and [[Recursion]] have "come to nothing", called Chomsky's idea that language arose as a result of a genetic mutation "utterly eccentric", and regretted that Chomsky "turned the discipline of syntactic theory into a personality cult". === Coinings === Pullum has coined or prompted the coining of a number of terms that have come to be popularly used including ''[[eggcorn]]'', ''[[snowclone]]'', and ''linguification''.{{Cite web |date=2020-12-18 |title=Denials
